questions.question: Why is the zero vector not used as a normal vector?
options: The zero vector is not in any vector space.
The zero vector always gives a unique plane.
The zero vector is not perpendicular to any vector, so it cannot be normal
A normal vector must be nonzero, fixing a perpendicular direction

questions.question: If a plane has direction vectors $v$ and $w$, what must a normal vector $n$ satisfy?
options: $n\cdot v=0$ and $n\cdot w=0$.
$n\cdot v=1$ and $n\cdot w=1$.

questions.question: Which vector is normal to the $xy$-plane?
Which vector is normal to the plane with equation $2x-y+3z=5$?
For the plane through $A=(1,0,0)$ with normal $n=(1,2,3)$, which equation is correct?
Why does a normal vector give a compact equation for a plane?
options: It removes the need for a point on the plane
It lists all points of the plane one by one.
It turns plane membership into orthogonality
It replaces a plane by a single point.

questions.question: If $n$ is normal to a plane, why is $3n$ also normal?
options: It changes the plane into a line.
It is normal only if $3n=0$.
Scaling by $3$ stops it from being perpendicular to the plane's directions
Nonzero scalar multiples keep the same perpendicular direction

questions.question: A plane has direction vectors $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,1)$. Which vector is normal to it?
Does the point $B=(2,1,1)$ lie on the plane through $A=(1,1,1)$ with normal $n=(1,0,1)$?
options: Yes, because $B-A=(1,0,0)$ has dot product $0$.
Yes, because the point has the same third coordinate as $A$.
No, because every point with $y=1$ is excluded.
No, because $n\cdot(B-A)=1\ne0$.

questions.question: Why does a normal vector not determine a unique plane by itself?
options: Parallel planes can share the same normal vector.
A normal vector already includes a base point.
A normal vector must be zero to determine a plane.
A normal vector is never perpendicular to a plane.

questions.question: A plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has normal vector $\boldsymbol{n}=(0,0,1)$ and contains the point $\boldsymbol{A}=(0,0,2)$. Which statement holds for every point $\boldsymbol{B}$ of this plane?
options: $\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}=2$
$\boldsymbol{n}\cdot\boldsymbol{B}=0$
$\boldsymbol{n}\cdot(\boldsymbol{B}-\boldsymbol{A})=2$
$\boldsymbol{B}$ is a multiple of $\boldsymbol{n}$
